propositions.text: This is the second judicial review application by Fan Zhang after visa officers refused her work permit application.
propositions.quote: This is the second application for judicial review brought by Fan Zhang in response to refusals by visa officers to accept her application for a work permit authorizing her arranged employment in Vancouver as a childcare worker.

propositions.text: The first refusal decision was set aside on consent of the parties.
propositions.quote: The first refusal decision was set aside on consent of the parties.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is Fan Zhang's second judicial review after visa refusals; the first refusal was set aside by consent.

propositions.text: The decision under review was made by an unidentified visa officer on March 27, 2019, denying Ms. Zhang's application.
propositions.quote: The decision that is the subject of this application was rendered by an unidentified visa officer (Officer) on March 27, 2019.

propositions.text: The Officer denied the application on two grounds: inability to perform work and risk of unauthorized overstay.
propositions.quote: Upon completion of an interview with Ms. Zhang, the Officer denied her application on two grounds: (a) that she had failed to establish that she was able to adequately perform the work required; and (b) that, based on her purpose for coming to Canada, she represented a risk of an unauthorized overstay;

propositions.text: The Officer expressed additional concerns about lack of paid experience, reasons for working as caregiver, and doubts about bona fide temporary worker status.
propositions.quote: The notes accompanying the Officer’s decision express the following additional concerns: In view of your lack of paid experience as a caregiver, the reasons you provided for why you want to work as a caregiver in Cda, and the plan you described, I am not satisfied that you meet the requirement for issuance of a work permit. I am not satisfied that you are a bona fide temporary worker.

propositions.text: The Officer was not satisfied Ms. Zhang was a genuine temporary worker or able to perform job duties, leading to refusal.
propositions.quote: Based on our conversation and information presented before me, I am not satisfied that you are a genuine temporary worker in Cda. I am also not satisfied that you demonstrated ability to perform duties required by the job offered in Cda. Your application is refused.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports the visa officer refused Ms. Zhang's application on grounds of work ability and risk of overstay, expressing additional concerns about experience and bona fide status.

propositions.text: Ms. Zhang argues the Officer's decision was unreasonable for ignoring reliable evidence of her qualifications and no risk of overstaying.
propositions.quote: Ms. Zhang argues that the Officer’s decision was unreasonable because it failed to account for reliable evidence that she was well qualified to perform the work required and that she did not represent a risk of overstaying the term of the requested visa.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Zhang argues the Officer's decision was unreasonable for ignoring evidence of her qualifications and no overstay risk.

propositions.text: The issues are evidence-based and assessed on reasonableness standard per Vavilov.
propositions.quote: The determinative issues raised by the Applicant are evidence-based and must be assessed on the standard of reasonableness.

propositions.text: Vavilov affirms judicial review focuses on decision-maker's reasons, not reweighing evidence, due to decision-maker's advantageous position.
propositions.quote: In Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, [2019] SCJ No 65 (QL), the Supreme Court of Canada recently affirmed that judicial review is primarily focussed on the reasons given by the decision-maker in support of its conclusion. This does not generally permit the reweighing and reassessing of evidence considered by the decision-maker, in part, because of its advantageous position (see para 125).

propositions.text: Reasonableness may be undermined if decision-maker misapprehended or failed to account for evidence or conclusions lack evidentiary basis.
propositions.quote: On the other hand, “the reasonableness of a decision may be jeopardized where the decision-maker has fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for the evidence before it”, or where its conclusions were not based on the evidence presented (see para 126).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the reasonableness standard from Vavilov, focusing on decision-maker's reasons and accounting for evidence properly.

propositions.text: Vavilov paras 127-128 discuss balance between deference and responsive reasons, requiring meaningful engagement with central issues.
propositions.quote: The balance to be achieved between the obligations of respectful deference and “responsive reasons” is further discussed at paras 127-128: [127] The principles of justification and transparency require that an administrative decision maker’s reasons meaningfully account for the central issues and concerns raised by the parties.

propositions.text: Responsive reasons show decision-maker listened; failure to address key issues may question alertness and fairness.
propositions.quote: The concept of responsive reasons is inherently bound up with this principle, because reasons are the primary mechanism by which decision makers demonstrate that they have actually listened to the parties.

propositions.text: Courts do not expect responses to every argument or explicit findings on every element; excessive expectations harm administrative function.
propositions.quote: Reviewing courts cannot expect administrative decision makers to “respond to every argument or line of possible analysis” (Newfoundland Nurses, at para. 25), or to “make an explicit finding on each constituent element, however subordinate, leading to its final conclusion” (para 16).

propositions.text: Failure to grapple with key issues may indicate flaws in reasoning and lack of sensitivity to the matter.
propositions.quote: However, a decision maker’s failure to meaningfully grapple with key issues or central arguments raised by the parties may call into question whether the decision maker was actually alert and sensitive to the matter before it.

propositions.text: Careful reasons assure parties their concerns were heard and help decision-maker identify reasoning flaws.
propositions.quote: In addition to assuring parties that their concerns have been heard, the process of drafting reasons with care and attention can alert the decision maker to inadvertent gaps and other flaws in its reasoning: Baker, at para. 39.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Vavilov on the need for meaningful, responsive reasons balancing deference and fairness, without requiring exhaustive findings.

propositions.text: The Officer's concerns about Ms. Zhang's intentions were unfocused and conflated employment plan doubts with overstay risk.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s concerns about Ms. Zhang’s intentions are, to the extent considered, unfocussed.

propositions.text: Having dual intent to pursue permanent residency is not concerning for temporary work permit.
propositions.quote: Ms. Zhang clearly expressed an intention to pursue permanent residency if it was available, but having a dual purpose is not a matter of any concern.

propositions.text: Misgivings about employment choices do not equate to risk of unauthorized overstay.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, misgivings about the wisdom of an applicant’s employment choices do not directly equate with the risk of an unauthorized overstay.

propositions.text: Ms. Zhang met all employment requirements and had an employment contract.
propositions.quote: What is clear from the record was that Ms. Zhang met all of the stipulated requirements of the proposed employment and had entered into an employment contract.

propositions.text: Nothing suggests Ms. Zhang did not intend or was unlikely to fulfill employment obligations.
propositions.quote: There is nothing in the record or in the Officer’s reasons suggesting that she did not intend or was unlikely to fulfill her employment obligations.

propositions.text: If Ms. Zhang aimed for permanent residency, she was unlikely to breach temporary worker conditions.
propositions.quote: Indeed, if her ultimate goal was to obtain permanent residency, it was unlikely she would breach the conditions of her initial entry into Canada as a temporary worker.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's concerns about Ms. Zhang's intentions unfocused and unsupported by evidence, noting dual intent is lawful.

propositions.text: The Officer may have been concerned about Ms. Zhang's English proficiency due to some misunderstandings during the interview.
propositions.quote: The Officer may also have been concerned about Ms. Zhang’s language proficiency, and it appears on the record she did have some difficulty understanding some questions.

propositions.text: Ms. Zhang asked for repetition and confused some words but answered well when simpler language was used.
propositions.quote: For instance, when the Officer asked if she was “currently employed”, she asked that the question be repeated... Overall, Ms. Zhang was reasonably responsive when the Officer employed simpler language.

propositions.text: Any doubts about English proficiency stemmed more from the Officer's question phrasing than Ms. Zhang's answers.
propositions.quote: To the extent that the Officer harboured any doubts about Ms. Zhang’s English proficiency, the problem was more in the initial framing of the questions posed by the Officer than in the answers she provided.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Ms. Zhang had some language difficulties but responded well to simpler questions; doubts stemmed from Officer's phrasing.

propositions.text: The Officer's concerns about overstay risk arose mainly from an interview exchange about Ms. Zhang's future intentions.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s stated reservations about the risk of an overstay arose mainly out of the following exchange about Ms. Zhang’s intentions for the future:

propositions.text: Ms. Zhang expressed willingness to try to finish her job and transfer employers if needed, and to stay in Canada.
propositions.quote: I know this situation can probably happen. I will try my best to finish my job... I will work. Maybe they will not extend, I will look for another employer.

propositions.text: The Officer expressed concern Ms. Zhang would not leave Canada after entry, questioning bona fide temporary worker status.
propositions.quote: I am concerned that you will not depart Cda once you enter. I am concerned that you are not a bona fide temporary worker.

propositions.text: Ms. Zhang said she planned to continue education in Canada after 2-3 years working as caregiver.
propositions.quote: Yes, temporary worker in Cda. After 2 or 3 years, I will continue my education in pre-school education.

propositions.text: The Officer noted Ms. Zhang could have applied for a study permit if she intended to study.
propositions.quote: If your intention is to study, you could have applied for a study permit.

propositions.text: Ms. Zhang explained working as caregiver would help her earn money to study abroad, avoiding financial burden on family.
propositions.quote: If I work as a caregiver, I can earn money and I can go to school. If I apply for a study visa, it is a financial burden for my family.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports the Officer's interview concerns about Ms. Zhang's intentions and overstay risk based on her answers about work and study plans.

propositions.text: Ms. Zhang's answers do not support concern about ulterior motive to remain without authorization.
propositions.quote: There is nothing in these answers remotely supporting a concern about an ulterior motive to remain in Canada without authorization.

propositions.text: Ms. Zhang's responses indicate she would maintain lawful immigration status and have dual lawful intent.
propositions.quote: Every one of Ms. Zhang’s responses indicated that she would take appropriate steps to preserve a lawful immigration status in Canada. Ms. Zhang’s answers reflect a dual but entirely lawful intent to obtain temporary worker status and thereafter to pursue available options to obtain permanent residency.

propositions.text: Bondoc case supports that visa officer must consider dual intent and ties to home country in assessing overstay risk.
propositions.quote: Her situation is markedly similar to the one described in Bondoc v Canada... The visa officer does not have to be satisfied that the applicant has a temporary purpose in coming to Canada, but instead that the applicant will not remain illegally in Canada if her application for permanent residence under the LIC class is rejected.

propositions.text: The Officer ignored factors detracting from suspicion: family in China, assets, lawful residence in England, no immigration problems, no family in Canada.
propositions.quote: Moreover, there were a number of considerations the Officer ignored that detracted from a suspicion that she represented a risk to remain in Canada without authorization. Her husband and child remained in China and she had family assets there... She had no family members in Canada.

propositions.text: Pisarevic case contrasts with Ms. Zhang's situation where ties were severed; here ties remain.
propositions.quote: This was unlike the situation in Pisarevic v Canada... where the applicant had severed all of his ties to his home country.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Ms. Zhang's answers show lawful dual intent and the Officer ignored relevant factors reducing overstay risk, citing Bondoc and Pisarevic.

propositions.text: The Officer's concerns about Ms. Zhang's childcare ability are misplaced; she was over-qualified.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s concerns about Ms. Zhang’s ability to carry out the childcare responsibilities of the proposed employment are similarly misplaced and unreasonable. If anything, Ms. Zhang was over-qualified for the job.

propositions.text: Ms. Zhang has a university degree, teaching experience, internship with disabled children, caregiver diploma, and raised her own child.
propositions.quote: She has a university degree and a lengthy history of employment as a teacher of Chinese traditional medicine. She successfully completed an internship in a Chinese kindergarten program with a focus on children with disabilities. More recently, she successfully completed a program for a diploma as an in-home Caregiver. She had also raised her own child.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's concerns about childcare ability unreasonable; Ms. Zhang was over-qualified with relevant education and experience.

propositions.text: The Officer ignored or discounted Ms. Zhang's accomplishments on spurious grounds, including unpaid experience and motherhood relevance.
propositions.quote: Most of these accomplishments were ignored completely by the Officer. To the extent that any are mentioned in the reasons, they are discounted on spurious grounds.

propositions.text: Motherhood responsibilities are relevant to childcare work, supported by Sibal case.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Officer’s suggestion that Ms. Zhang’s responsibilities as a mother were somehow irrelevant to working as a paid childcare provider to another child is illogical: see Sibal v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 159, 302 ACWS (3d) 376, at paras 39-43.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer ignored or discounted Ms. Zhang's relevant experience and motherhood, citing Sibal to support relevance.

propositions.text: The Officer had a legal duty to consider all evidence and not selectively rely on only refusal-supporting evidence.
propositions.quote: The Officer had a legal obligation to engage with all of the evidence and not to selectively choose only those things that supported a refusal.

propositions.text: Speculative suspicions about motives or employment wisdom do not justify refusal against reliable contrary evidence.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, suspicions based largely, if not wholly, on speculation about an applicant’s motives or about the wisdom of taking on low-paid child care employment do not provide a reasonable foundation for a negative decision when measured against reliable actual evidence supporting the opposite conclusion.

propositions.text: Per Vavilov para 126, failure to account for significant relevant evidence renders decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: This decision is unreasonable for the reason that it fails to account for a significant body of relevant evidence that supported the granting of a visa: see Vavilov at para. 126.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds the Officer failed legal duty by selectively considering evidence and relying on speculation, making the decision unreasonable per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Ms. Zhang argues the Court should direct the Minister to grant a work visa due to delays and jeopardy to employment.
propositions.quote: Ms. Zhang argues that in the face of two deficient decisions, the Court should now direct the Minister to grant a work visa. She points out that her application has been held up for two years and her arranged employment is in jeopardy.

propositions.text: The Court does not accept that extraordinary relief of granting a visa is appropriate given changing factual circumstances.
propositions.quote: I do not accept that the Court should, in these circumstances, grant that form of extraordinary relief.

propositions.text: The visa award is not inevitable due to possible changes in employment or health status.
propositions.quote: this is a decision that is dependant on a potentially changing factual landscape where Ms. Zhang’s continuing eligibility is not assured. For instance, with the passage of time, her arranged employment could lapse or her health status could change.

propositions.text: The Minister is expected to prioritize reconsideration of Ms. Zhang's case due to prior mishandling.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, given the mishandling of this application on two occasions, I expect the Minister to give the reconsideration of this case priority.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Zhang asks for visa grant; court refuses but expects Minister to prioritize reconsideration due to prior mishandling.

propositions.text: This application does not warrant costs.
propositions.quote: This is also not an application that warrants costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court orders no costs for this application.

propositions.text: The application is allowed and the matter is to be redetermined by a different decision-maker.
propositions.quote: THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that this application is allowed with the matter to be redetermined on the merits and in conformity with these reasons by a different decision-maker.

propositions.text: No certified question was proposed and no issue of general importance arises.
propositions.quote: Neither party proposed a certified question and no issue of general importance arises on this record.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the application, orders redetermination by a different decision-maker, and notes no certified question or general issue.
